newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmer road blocks spread, general unrest.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmer road blocks spread, general unrest.

text.p: Greece's socialist government faced mounting protests against its economic policies on Sunday with farmers blockading main north-south road and rail links for the fourth day and an array of other groups planning strikes.
The farmers rejected a request by government officials over the weekend to give up their crippling blockade for a week while both sides tried to negotiate a settlement.
"Fuel costs have gone up and our prices have gone down. You can see for yourself the mess we're in," said Theodoros Zafiropoulos, president of the northern farm town of Kipseli.

Protests against the 1997 budget submitted on Friday have been growing. Strikes have been called for the coming week by prison wardens, pensioners, teachers, port and tax officials, construction workers and the civil servants union.
A motley fleet of some 5,000 farm tractors has seized toll booths and barricaded the main north-south national road as well as rail links throughout the central Thessely farming region.
Fires blazed through the night to stave off the cold and rain. Tents were thrown up among the sea of tractors choking Thessaly roads and towns.
Only army, police or emergency transport was allowed to pass the farmers' barricades.

The protest has effectively cut land links between Athens and the country's second city, the northern port of Salonika. The north-south land links are the main means of transporting goods and produce between the two cities.

The farmers, many flying black flags or banners proclaiming "Don't Give In" from their tractors, branched out on sideroads between Larissa and Salonika to stop trucks, buses and motorists from skirting the main highway, police said.

Convoys of commercial trucks began to line the highway. Farm officials were threatening to extend the blockade to other parts of Greece, especially the Peloponnese farm area and the Western Agrinion region.
A similar farm protest in March 1995 lasted for 10 days and sent food prices skyrocketing and crippled international road transport.

Farmers want lower fuel costs, a cut in Value Added Tax (VAT) on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and rescheduling $1.3 billion in farm debts owed to the state Agricultural Bank.
Government officials, including Deputy Agriculture Minister Dimitris Sotirlis, went to the centre of the farm rebellion in Larissa and said they were willing to make compromises.
But they said there was no question of squeezing more money out of the 1997 budget for Greek agriculture.

"We have listened to government promises before, especially in 1995. They were never honoured. This time we will block the highway until Christmas. We have nothing to lose," said Mihalis Georgios, a farmers' representative in Larissa.
The 1997 budget set out tough targets to put the economy on track for convergence with Greece's European Union partners by the turn of the century.
Spending was cut, taxes hiked and an array of tax exemptions dumped. Greece's largest labour unions held a 24-hour nationwide strike on Thursday to protest against the budget.

So far Prime Minister Costas Simitis has held to a tough line and rejected demands by most groups, saying Greece must put its economic house in order and achieve full economic and monetary union with its EU partners by 2001.
